content:
Playing golf with gcongr in mathlib (see #37462), a few small enhancements come to my mind. Are there any reasons not to implement any of the following? CC @Jovan Gerbscheid @Heather Macbeth

  • it's not very often, but not rarely useful to add assumption as a discharger for side goals (I'd do so after the existing positivity discharger)

• many proofs are gcongr; exact foo or perhaps gcongr; exacts [foo, bar] (perhaps split into exacts). We could have syntactic sugar for this, to several degrees:
    • simplest one: gcongr using foo (taking one expression) is equivalent to gcongr; exact foo
    • medium: gcongr using foo, bar (taking a list of expressions) is equivalent to gcongr; exact [foo, bar]
    • hard: allow passing terms for a subset of goals --- e.g., if there are 3 goals left after gcongr, then gcongr using foo, bar will address the first two and leave the third.

The using syntax is analogous to filter_upwards or simpa (so seems logical to me).
I'm sure the first one would be good, the second one also. I'm less sure if the last one is as useful; we also have e.g. three goals, with the middle term being a different tactic.

• We could allow passing additional terms to gcongr, that are created as haves before running gcongr, as in gcongr [hz i t]. This is already supported in positivity and finiteness, and could e.g. allow positivity to discharge more side goals.
    I think this would be unlikely to do harm, but am more on the fence if this is useful already.

Here are two ideas I had:

  • We want to separate side goals from main goals. So, it would be neat to have a syntax gcongr by ... where the nested by block gets the side goals. This makes gcongr proofs nicer to read, because it is clear which goal came from where.
  • To extend the above even more, we could have a special syntax for filling in main subgoals: gcongr $(my_proof) + $(other_proof) could be short for gcongr; exacts [my_proof, other_proof]. But the advantage is that you can see exactly the structure of which proof is used for what subgoal.
The reason to use tactics for side goals rather than a term proof is that it's not always obvious what the side goals will be, and we need a tactic state in order to see the side goals.
What do you think about these @Michael Rothgang?
(Note that I have the open PR #36314 (support rintro patterns in gcongr) which I'd like to have merged before doing any of these proposed enhancements, to avoid annoying merge conflicts.)

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

(Note that I have the open PR #36314 (support rintro patterns in gcongr) which I'd like to have merged before doing any of these proposed enhancements, to avoid annoying merge conflicts.)

Adding gcongr dischargers can be separate from these, but otherwise I agree.
Separating main and side goals sounds useful for me; that is indeed intransparent now!
I'm not sure how well a by block will work for several sidegoals, but we can certainly try (and perhaps these will become more and more rare if we add better dischargers :-)).

I'm not sure if $(my_proof) is the most readable syntax yet (perhaps using my_proof + other_proof or some variant thereof is better? But that's bikeshedding which can happen on an implementation PR, so we have actual examples to look at :-)
Overall: I like your ideas; that's a more refined approach than mine!

Is it possible to have gcongr macro? Just like congr macro. For example:

import Mathlib

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h1 : a ≤ b) (h2 : c < d) : True := by
  have h3 := gcongr($(h1) + $(h2))
  sorry

In principle, a gcongr(...) elaborator would be possible. Though its implementation would be mostly disjoint from that of the gcongr tactic. (The difference is that the gcongr tactic does backwards reasoning, while a gcongr(...) term elaborator would do forwards reasoning)

The dollar in the $(my_proof) syntax is necessary for Lean to separate the proof term from the gcongr pattern (recall that both the pattern and the proof can be arbitrary expressions). And dollar symbols are the standard way in Lean to do this kind of quotation inside expressions.

The idea for a by block for side goals came from this discussion: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/270676-lean4/topic/Design.20of.20tactics.20that.20create.20side.20goals/with/539432664

Do you have other ideas for a syntax for dealing with side goals?

the dollars usually signify disquotations, no? as in, foo is an identifier '(ident|foo) is a Syntax object representing the identifier, and '(ident|$foo + 1) is a syntax object representing composing whatever the syntax object foo is with the operation of + 1?

those semantics aside, i have to say i find the proposed gcongr $(my_proof) + $(other_proof) notation confusing. your description suggests to me that there need not be any + involved in the goal?
I think the "use the following proofs" idea has been frequently implemented in syntax just as taking a list of proof terms, and that seems to work just fine for tactics like simp, grind, rw, etc... i don't see why we would break that pattern for the gcongr tactic?

this "focused side goals" syntax can perhaps follow the with syntax pattern? i.e. something like

example : Foo := by
  gcongr with
  | a < b => sorry
  | _ => sorry
Oh, no I meant the + as mimicking the shape of the goal. So if the goal is a + 2 * b < c + 2 * d, you might write a proof as gcongr $h1 + 2 * $h2.
i see... i still don't think i like it... seeing disquotations outside of quotations seems weird...

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

  • gcongr $(my_proof) + $(other_proof) could be short for gcongr; exacts [my_proof, other_proof].

btw, this doesn't suggest that the "mimicing the shape of the goal" would be enforced by the tactic, hence my confusion.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

Oh, no I meant the + as mimicking the shape of the goal. So if the goal is a + 2 * b < c + 2 * d, you might write a proof as gcongr $h1 + 2 * $h2.

I think this (as well as the $(my_proof) + $(other_proof)) is just the forward reasoning version gcongr($(h1) + 2 * $(h2)).
So maybe the proof becomes exact gcongr($(h1) + 2 * $(h2)) or refine gcongr($(?_) + 2 * $(?_))?

No, the gcongr tactic should do backwards reasoning. Note that it is already possible to write gcongr ?_ + 2 * ?_. On the other hand, the term gcongr($(?_) + 2 * $(?_)) doesn't make much sense, because you don't know which relation should be used (unless you make use of the expected type and then do backwards reasoning instead of forwards reasoning).
Making use of the expected type seems like a reasonable thing to me...

Jz Pan said:

Is it possible to have gcongr macro? Just like congr macro. For example:

import Mathlib

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h1 : a ≤ b) (h2 : c < d) : True := by
  have h3 := gcongr($(h1) + $(h2))
  sorry

But a gcongr(...) term elaborator needs to use forwards reasoning (and hence not make use of the expected type) if you want to support this.

Or do you think it would be acceptable if the relation would have to be specified manually? As in

import Mathlib

example (a b c d : ℝ) (h1 : a ≤ b) (h2 : c < d) : True := by
  have h3 : _ < _ := gcongr($(h1) + $(h2))
  sorry

I think it could figure out automatically that ≤ + < = <, ≤ + ≤ = ≤, isn't it? Just like calc which will figure out automatically that a ≤ b, b < c => a < c, a ≤ b, b ≤ c => a ≤ c, by tagging appropriate theorems with @[trans].

Well, that depends on whether you do forwards or backwards reasoning. The gcongr implementation uses backwards reasoning, which means that it starts by looking at the outermost relation.

To support the forwards reasoning as you describe, we would have to write a new implementation from scratch.

Note that grw currently piggy backs on the implementation of gcongr, but I'm working on a new implementation (which I'm calling gsimp for now) which is implemented separately from gcongr. So that gives a total of 3 different potential implementation of generalized congruence :sweat_smile:
